accuracy.evidence: Follows CCSS W.6-8.1 parts (claim, reasons, relevant evidence, counterclaim, transitions, formal style, concluding statement); evidence examples are real: Seattle 2016 later-start study and the LSE 91-school phone study.

misconceptions.evidence: Adult text names fact-as-claim, anecdote or 'everyone knows' as evidence, ignoring or conceding to the other side, straw-man attacks, slang and a new point in the conclusion; lab MISS and why() answer each.

lab_distinct.evidence: Builds one five-paragraph argument piece by piece and then orders the paragraphs; unlike the audience/tone lab (flagaud), the craft-vocabulary lab, or the author-purpose lab (flagpurp).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each correct choice fills the live essay card for that paragraph, so the learner watches the argument assemble and sees why each part (rebuttal, connective, conclusion) has a distinct job.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions (what a claim is, whether one story is strong evidence, where the counterclaim goes) are tested by the choices and the ordering that follow, with spot-on or rethink feedback.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven new challenge questions on other issues (homework, phones, policy); every wrong option has a specific why() message, for example that copying the opening adds nothing to a conclusion.

readability.evidence: Kid text opens with the later-bedtime example and uses short sentences; adult text was simplified until validate_lessons rated it at or below the FK grade 10 target while keeping the curriculum terms.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph either names an argument part and its job, a named mistake, or what the lab does; the family tip is a concrete claim, reasons and counterclaim exercise on a real family debate.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 light and 360x640 Android dark screenshots show five readable essay cards with wrapped text, full-width answer buttons below, and no horizontal overflow at any step.

accessibility.evidence: All choices are buttons; ordering works by tapping a card or its button twin; the canvas aria-label repeats each prompt and result, and walk.cjs axe passed in both themes.

sources: Common Core State Standards ELA W.6.1, W.7.1, W.8.1 (a-e)
UK National Curriculum 2013, KS3 English programme of study: Writing (formal expository essays and arguments)
Dunster et al. 2018, Science Advances: Sleepmore in Seattle; Beland and Murphy 2016, Labour Economics: Ill Communication (phone bans)
